proposals.name: Names the causal mechanism behind a known failure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract identifies WHY an existing phenomenon or failure occurs — a specific mechanism, and then derives the fix from that mechanism. Score 5 if a mechanism is gestured at but the method is not visibly derived from it. Score 0 if the abstract only reports that a method works better, with the cause of the prior failure unexamined.
proposals.rationale: R14 explicitly contrasts 'clues from the outcome' with 'finding out the causing factor' and derives the auxiliary skip connection from the diagnosis; R05 diagnoses adversarial training as converging to a degenerate minimum with curvature artifacts and builds both a new attack and a defense from that. Both are dense-high/card-low. By contrast R24 and R52 propose refinements without a diagnosis and are card-high.

proposals.name: Overturns or qualifies a widely held belief
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract states a belief the field currently holds and presents evidence or theory that the belief is false, unnecessary, or narrower than assumed. 5 = positions against prior work only as 'existing methods have limitation X'. 0 = purely additive; no incumbent belief is put at risk.
proposals.rationale: R40 says outright 'we challenge the commonly-held beliefs by showing that none of the perceived benefits is unique to normalization'; R45 argues against the assumed source of DNN gains and reports that DNNs cannot extrapolate. Both dense-high/card-low, while incremental-improvement abstracts like R43 and R27 are card-high.

proposals.name: Reports a limitation or negative result against own claim
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract explicitly reports a finding that weakens, bounds, or partly undoes its own contribution (a regime where the method fails, a subsequent refutation, a cost paid). 5 = a mild scoping caveat. 0 = no cost, boundary, or failure of the proposal is stated anywhere.
proposals.rationale: R05 closes with 'subsequent work found that more elaborate black-box attacks could significantly enhance transferability and reduce the accuracy of our models'; R53 ends by demonstrating 'the limits of our FA variant when the number of output neurons grows'. Both dense-high/card-low — a scorecard reading for claimed strength penalizes exactly this honesty.

proposals.name: Simplicity of mechanism relative to size of effect
proposals.instruction: 10 = the described intervention is small, cheap, and easy to state (an initialization rule, one extra connection, one loss term) yet is claimed to change a large or hard outcome. 0 = the effect claimed is modest while the machinery required is elaborate, multi-component, or requires several new sub-variants.
proposals.rationale: R40 (rescaled initialization → 10,000-layer training without normalization) and R30 (plain filter pruning, works with existing BLAS, no sparse libraries) are dense-high/card-low. R24, which stacks SSFG then MSSFG then PSSFG variants, and R52's multi-loss framework are card-high — the scorecard credits machinery per se.

proposals.name: Method-to-benchmark ratio: substance vs. benchmark listing
proposals.instruction: Score the balance. 10 = conceptual content dominates and benchmarks are cited only as sufficient evidence. 0 = the abstract's persuasive weight rests on an enumeration of datasets, numbers, and 'state-of-the-art' claims with little said about why the method should work.
proposals.rationale: R08 (card_pct 1.00) and R52 (card .968) are dominated by dataset/benchmark enumeration and percentage gains; R21 and R33, both dense-high/card-low, carry almost no benchmark listing but heavy conceptual content.

proposals.name: Unifies or subsumes prior methods as special cases
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract shows that several previously separate methods, objectives, or models fall out of its framework as special cases or limits. 5 = it draws a loose analogy to one prior line. 0 = it is one more member of an existing family with no reduction of prior work.
proposals.rationale: R21 recovers 'many of the models that were previously discussed in the literature, e.g. Hopfield Networks is All You Need' by integrating out hidden neurons (dense-high/card-low); R47 also claims unification and is card-high, so the criterion must reward demonstrated derivation (R21) over asserted unification (R47).

proposals.name: New problem formulation, not new method for old problem
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract defines a task, setting, or resource that did not previously exist and argues why it is needed. 5 = a known problem in a new domain. 0 = a new method evaluated entirely on established tasks.
proposals.rationale: R06 introduces open QA over tables AND text 'for the first time' with a new dataset; R17 builds ALFWorld to join abstract text policies to embodied execution. Both dense-high/card-low, while card-high rows R26, R27, R43 all operate inside a fully established problem.

proposals.name: Baseline difficulty is calibrated and honestly low
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract reports how hard the problem is, including a baseline that performs poorly, and reports its own still-imperfect number. 0 = only final favorable numbers appear, with no evidence the task is difficult or the headroom is real.
proposals.rationale: R06 volunteers that its baseline gets exact match under 10% and its improved system reaches only 27% — dense-high/card-low. R52's four bolded mAP gains and R08's 'new state-of-the-art error' carry no difficulty calibration and are card-high.

proposals.name: Theory that explains an existing empirical puzzle
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract names a concrete, previously reported empirical inconsistency and provides analysis that resolves it, with the analysis then checked empirically. 5 = theory developed in the abstract with no tie to a reported puzzle. 0 = theory or experiment alone with no bridge between them.
proposals.rationale: R33 opens on 'mixed empirical results when extrapolating' and identifies conditions reconciling MLP failure with GNN success, verified empirically; R60 explains why stacking GCN layers hurts, then derives weight-scaling guidance and confirms it. Both dense-high/card-low, while pure-theory rows R41 and R23 sit card-high relative to dense.

proposals.name: Actionable guidance a practitioner could apply tomorrow
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract yields a concrete prescription (an initialization, a normalization rule, a design choice) usable outside the paper's own system. 0 = the result is confined to the authors' specific model and offers no transferable rule.
proposals.rationale: R60 'provides principled guidelines for weight normalization of graph NNs'; R30 stresses compatibility with existing dense BLAS libraries so no special infrastructure is needed. Both dense-high/card-low.

proposals.name: Promotional register without matching specificity
proposals.instruction: Reverse-scored. 10 = claims are stated plainly and every strong adjective is backed by a specific quantity or mechanism in the same abstract. 0 = the text leans on 'novel', 'impressive', 'well-proven', 'extensive', 'significant', 'drastically', 'superior' as substitutes for saying what was done or measured.
proposals.rationale: R43 uses 'a well-proven measure', 'impressive results', 'extensive experiments' throughout and is card .790 vs dense .758; R24 repeats 'extensive experiments... favorable performance' and is card .452 vs dense .226. The scorecard appears to read confident register as strength.

proposals.name: Scope of claim matches the evidence offered
proposals.instruction: 10 = the generality asserted in the framing is exactly what the reported evidence supports. 0 = a sweeping claim ('any network', 'general setting', 'broad family') is supported only by narrow or small-scale evidence, or a genuinely broad result is undersold to the point of being unassessable.
proposals.rationale: R11 claims 'the general setting where explicit labels are difficult to obtain' from synthetic 2D sequences plus vehicle motion (dense-low/card-high); R07 claims 'the first attack-independent robustness metric that can be applied to any neural network classifier' on the strength of correlational agreement with attack norms (dense-low/card-high).

proposals.name: Robustness or generality is demonstrated across regimes, not one setting
proposals.instruction: 10 = the same fixed method is shown to hold across genuinely different task families, scales, or conditions, with sameness of configuration made explicit. 5 = several datasets from one family. 0 = a single benchmark, or many benchmarks that differ only cosmetically.
proposals.rationale: R50 makes this explicit — 'the same learning algorithm, network architecture and hyper-parameters' over 20+ physics tasks — and R54 spans locomotion tasks from raw kinematics. This is one axis where dense and card largely agree at the top, so it isolates what genuine breadth looks like versus the mere dataset-listing penalized in A05.

proposals.name: Composite: precise problem statement together with matching contribution
proposals.instruction: Judge both halves. 10 = the abstract states a sharply specified obstacle (with the quantity, regime, or failure mode named) AND the contribution is visibly the thing that removes that obstacle. 5 = one half present. 0 = a generic motivation ('X is important; however, challenges remain') followed by a contribution whose connection to the stated obstacle is unstated.
proposals.rationale: R10 names the obstacle exactly (PSRNNs need too many random features; ORF theory does not cover the kernel ridge regression step) and extends the theory to close precisely that gap — dense-high/card-low. R32 states a generic 'MI is intractable' framing and proposes a generic improvement — dense .161 vs card .452.

proposals.name: Composite: rigor/reproducibility work paired with a substantive finding
proposals.instruction: 10 = the abstract does methodological or evaluative housekeeping (re-evaluation, controlled comparison, new metric, diagnostic suite) AND reports a substantive discovery that follows from it. 5 = careful methodology with no discovery beyond 'prior comparisons were unfair'. 0 = neither.
proposals.rationale: R34 runs 47,000 controlled experiments and additionally finds that structure-agnostic baselines match GNNs on some datasets — yet sits dense .742 / card .871, suggesting the scorecard credits the scale of the audit; R59 similarly is card .774 / dense .548 for building an evaluation suite. This criterion forces the judge to separate the audit's size from what the audit actually revealed.

proposals.name: Named-acronym branding of the proposed method
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text coins and repeatedly uses a proper-noun name or capitalised acronym for the proposed method (e.g. an all-caps token, a backronym spelled out in parentheses, a playful nickname), counting how prominently and how often that coined name is repeated. 0 = no coined name, the method is only described functionally; 10 = a memorable coined name introduced early and repeated many times. Judge only the presence and prominence of the naming device, not whether the naming is apt, clever, or whether the method is good.
proposals.rationale: Named-acronym branding is a stylistic house habit, not evidence of contribution. R51 ('CLEVER, which is short for Cross Lipschitz Extreme Value for nEtwork Robustness') and R36 ('tent') and R42 ('VADA', 'DIRT-T') carry heavy branding; R30 and R15 describe methods with no coined name at all. Both models can key on nameability rather than substance.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice/marketing habit in the abstract format (lab branding conventions)

proposals.name: Density of named benchmark and architecture tokens
proposals.instruction: Count and score 0-10 the extent to which the text is packed with named datasets, benchmarks, and architecture names (e.g. ImageNet, CIFAR-10/100, MNIST, VGG-16, ResNet, Market/Duke, WMT, Atari). 0 = no named benchmark or architecture tokens; 10 = many distinct named benchmarks and architectures appearing repeatedly. Score only the count/density of such proper-noun tokens relative to text length; do not judge whether these are the right benchmarks or whether the evaluation is adequate.
proposals.rationale: A criterion bank scoring 'is it evaluated broadly' will reward token density mechanically. R05 and R41 list many benchmark/architecture names and sit card-high; R19 and R46, which are purely theoretical and name none, sit card-low. Density of proper nouns is a lexical artifact of subfield convention, not quality.

proposals.name: Numeric-result specificity: explicit percentages and deltas
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the text consists of explicit quantitative outcome statements — percentage figures, point deltas, speed-up multipliers, scores given to one or more decimals. 0 = no numbers reported at all; 10 = many precise figures, deltas and multipliers stated throughout. Score only the amount and precision of numeric reporting present in the text; do not judge whether the numbers are impressive, correct, or well-supported.
proposals.rationale: Explicit numbers are exactly what a checklist rubric rewards regardless of whether the numbers mean anything. R22 ('14.4%, 18.2%, 13.1% and 16.4% mAP') and R09 ('5x and 2x ... less than 0.6% top-5') are both card-high; R08 and R29, which report no figures, are card-low. Numeric verbosity is a writing convention of applied subfields.

proposals.name: Abstract length and clause elaboration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the sheer length and syntactic elaboration of the text: total word count, number of sentences, average sentence length, and use of multi-clause enumerations. 0 = a title only or one or two short sentences; 10 = a long, densely subordinated multi-paragraph-length abstract. Score length and elaboration only; do not judge whether the length is warranted or whether more content indicates a better paper.
proposals.rationale: Length is the classic verbosity confound and both models can absorb it. R40 is a title plus the two-word fragment 'International audience'; R01 is a bare title; R27, R41 and R07 run many hundreds of words. Rank differences across these are partly a length artifact rather than a quality signal.

proposals.name: Truncated or metadata-broken record fingerprint
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text shows signs of being an incomplete or corrupted record rather than a full abstract: title with no body, placeholder or repository-metadata strings (e.g. 'International audience'), a leading literal 'Abstract:' label, stray HTML entities (e.g. '&'), broken hyphenation or missing spaces between words. 0 = clean, complete prose; 10 = clearly truncated or littered with extraction artifacts. Score only the visible artifact/truncation evidence; do not judge whether the underlying work is good.
proposals.rationale: This is a property of how the record was scraped, not of the research. R40 has body text 'International audience'; R01 has no body at all; R43 begins with a literal 'Abstract:' label; R44 contains '&'; R13 has 'unstruc-tured', 'ourmodelcan', 'can bedirectly'. Any model keying on completeness is scoring the ingestion pipeline.
proposals.upstream_parent: corpus ingestion pipeline / source repository of the record

proposals.name: Public code/artifact release announcement
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text advertises released artifacts: a code URL, repository link, project page, or a sentence stating that code, data, models or videos are available. 0 = no mention of any released artifact; 10 = an explicit URL plus a prominent availability statement. Score only the presence and prominence of the release announcement; do not judge whether releasing code is good practice or whether the artifact would be useful.
proposals.rationale: Release statements are a proxy for the producing group's engineering resources and house norms, and they leave an unmistakable textual trace. R04 ends with a github.com/Meituan-AutoML URL, R22 with github.com/yxgeee/MMT, R41 with a github link, R57 with 'alfworld.github.io'; R19, R46, R28 have none. A rubric line item for reproducibility collapses into detecting a URL.
proposals.upstream_parent: producing group's resources and engineering norms (industry lab vs small group)

proposals.name: Insider citation-and-lineage naming inside the abstract
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text names prior work inside the abstract itself — author-year citations (e.g. 'Downey et al.', 'Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015'), named prior systems positioned as the parent of this work, or quoted titles of prior papers. 0 = no prior work named; 10 = several explicit author-year citations and named predecessor systems woven through the text. Score only how much prior-work naming is present; do not judge whether the citations are appropriate or whether being connected to prior work is good.
proposals.rationale: Citing by name inside an abstract is a habit of authors already inside a lineage; it signals network position and leaves a clean trace. R07 names 'Downey et al.', 'Smola et al.', 'Choromanski et al.'; R08 quotes the title 'Hopfield Networks is All You Need'; R42 cites 'Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015'; R12 cites 'Trouillon et al., 2016'; R57 cites 'Cote et al., 2018' and 'Shridhar et al., 2020'. Contrast R28, R46, R56, which name nobody.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's embeddedness in the subfield / seniority and network position

proposals.name: Explicit state-of-the-art / first-ever superiority claiming
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text contains explicit superiority and priority language: 'state-of-the-art', 'outperforms', 'significantly better', 'for the first time', 'to the best of our knowledge the first', 'unprecedented', 'extensive experiments verify'. Count occurrences and how emphatically they are phrased. 0 = no such claims anywhere; 10 = repeated, emphatic SOTA/priority/superiority claiming. Score only the amount of superiority-claiming language; explicitly do NOT judge whether the claims are justified or whether the work is actually strong.
proposals.rationale: This is submission rhetoric that a criterion bank can barely distinguish from evidence. R03 ('performs significantly better than state-of-the-art'), R11 ('To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work'), R55 ('unprecedented quality'), R48 ('Extensive experiments demonstrate the superior performance') all lean hard on it; R15 and R29 ('We show some evidence') are markedly hedged. The lexical register, not the evidence, is what is scored.
proposals.upstream_parent: venue-submission rhetoric norms and coaching received by the author

proposals.name: Enumerated-contributions template scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text uses explicit list scaffolding to package its content: 'our contributions are three-fold', numbered items '(i)/(ii)/(iii)' or '1)/2)', 'First ... Second ... Finally ...', 'On one hand ... On the other hand ...', or a rhetorical question posed and then answered. 0 = flowing prose with no enumerative scaffolding; 10 = a fully templated, explicitly numbered contribution list. Score only the presence and completeness of the template scaffolding; do not judge whether the structure makes the paper better or clearer.
proposals.rationale: Template scaffolding is a learned formatting habit that a rubric reads as organisation. R38 ('Our contributions are three-fold: (i) ... (ii) ... (iii)'), R41 ('On one hand ... On the other hand'), R10 ('first ... Second ... Finally'), R23 (poses '(i)' and '(ii)' questions), R48 ('(1) ... (2)') are heavily scaffolded, while R43, R52, R55 are unscaffolded prose. Scaffolding tracks who was taught the template.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the abstract format / writing templates circulating in a lab or a submission-advice culture

proposals.name: Late-arriver framing: repairs a crowded, already-named literature
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent to which the text positions itself as arriving AFTER an established and crowded body of work on the same topic rather than opening a topic: markers include phrases such as 'recent advances', 'a large stream of works', 'existing methods', 'state-of-the-art methods ignored X', 'despite the fast development of', 'previous works report mixed results', 'the common practice is', and framings that fix, unify, re-evaluate, stabilise, or fairly compare things others already built. Contrast with 0 = the text introduces a problem or setting as if little or nothing exists yet, defining terms from scratch and naming no crowd of predecessors. 10 = the text is explicitly a corrective, unifying, or robustifying response to a named and already-saturated line of work. Score only how strongly the late-arriver framing is present in the wording; do not judge whether arriving late or early is better, and do not judge the merit of the correction.
proposals.rationale: MODE-3 channel: an item's position late in a crowded topic stream forces a distinctive corrective register, and that register — not the science — may drive both models. R04 ('Despite the fast development of DARTS ... Existing robustifying methods draw clues from the outcome'), R34 ('a large stream of works ... re-evaluate five popular models'), R22 ('State-of-the-art methods ... ignored' the label noise), R06 ('Previous works report mixed empirical results'), R08 (reconciling several already-published models) all read as late arrivals; R43, R39, R29, R56 read as early, obvious-first readings of their problem. The crowdedness of the container is unobservable, but this wording is its fingerprint.
proposals.upstream_parent: position of the submission in the stream of entries on that topic (how crowded the subarea already is at submission time, and how late this entry lands in it)

proposals.name: Root-cause diagnosis vs. symptom patching
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract identifies and addresses an underlying causal mechanism behind a known failure (naming *why* it happens), rather than proposing a heuristic that reacts to symptoms or thresholds. Score 0 if the fix is a threshold/indicator/heuristic with no stated causal account.
proposals.rationale: R26 (DARTS-) explicitly contrasts itself with 'indicator'-based fixes and instead identifies skip-connections as the causing factor; R12 (Fixup) attributes normalization's effects to a specific gradient-scaling mechanism rather than treating it as a black-box trick. Both score very high dense (.968, 1.0) despite one having only moderate card score.

proposals.name: Refutes a prevailing assumption with evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract states it challenges, disproves, or overturns a widely-held belief/assumption and backs this with a concrete result. Score 0 if the abstract makes no such claim and simply improves a metric incrementally.
proposals.rationale: R12 (Fixup) explicitly says it 'challenges the commonly-held beliefs' about normalization; R59 (Tent) implicitly overturns the assumption that adaptation needs training data/retraining. Both are strong dense outliers (dense .968, .871) relative to more conventional-sounding submissions like R44 or R48.

proposals.name: Self-aware disclosure of limitations or failure modes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract itself names a concrete limitation, negative result, or scenario where the method fails/was later beaten, without being prompted. Score 0 if the abstract is uniformly self-promotional with no caveat.
proposals.rationale: R20 (Ensemble Adversarial Training) candidly notes 'subsequent work found... could significantly enhance transferability and reduce the accuracy of our models'; R56 states 'we demonstrate the limits of our FA variant.' Both carry high dense percentiles (.935, .355 relatively high vs its low card .129) suggesting this candor reads as credibility to a holistic reader but may not map to any card checklist item.

proposals.name: Unifies or generalizes prior disparate methods
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly shows that several previously separate techniques are special cases of, or are unified by, the proposed framework. Score 0 if the work is a standalone method with no connection drawn to other lines of work.
proposals.rationale: R49 (Probabilistic Formulation of Unsupervised Text Style Transfer) explicitly unifies backtranslation and adversarial-loss objectives under one probabilistic view; R41 (ReLIC) generalizes contrastive learning via a causal framework. Both are dense_low_card_high with large gaps (R49 dense .677/card .919), suggesting the scorecard over-credits unification-flavored abstracts that dense treats more skeptically, or under different weighting — worth isolating.

proposals.name: Crispness of the central claim
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract can be summarized in one clear sentence naming a single mechanism/idea driving the results. Score 0 if the abstract reads as a list of loosely related tweaks/variants with no single unifying idea.
proposals.rationale: R59 (Tent) and R12 (Fixup) each hinge on one crisp idea (minimize prediction entropy at test time; rescale initialization). R16 (SSFG/MSSFG/PSSFG) instead enumerates three sequential variants without one throughline, and shows a large dense_low_card_high gap (dense .226, card .355) — the card may reward the enumeration of contributions while dense discounts unfocused ones.

proposals.name: Minimalism: removes machinery rather than adding it
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed solution simplifies the pipeline (fewer moving parts, no extra stage/loss/network) relative to the status quo it targets. Score 0 if the method stacks new modules, losses, or training stages onto an already complex pipeline.
proposals.rationale: R12 (Fixup) removes normalization layers entirely; R59 (Tent) needs no retraining, just one epoch of test-time optimization. Both score much higher on dense than typical multi-module contributions like R16 or R31 (Mutual Mean-Teaching, which stacks two networks, two loss types, and online/offline label refinement).

proposals.name: Benchmark-anchored, calibratable numeric result
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract reports a number tied to a benchmark an ML expert can instantly calibrate against (e.g., named leaderboard rank, standard dataset accuracy delta, recognizable competition placement). Score 0 if all numeric claims are relative/vague ('order of magnitude', 'significant improvement') with no anchor.
proposals.rationale: R2 anchors results to KGS Go Server dan ranks and a named tournament placement; R57 (ProGAN) cites an inception score of 8.80 on CIFAR-10 and 1024^2 CelebA. These concrete, calibratable numbers likely drive dense perception of quality even where card treats numeric density generically.

proposals.name: Counterintuitive empirical or theoretical finding stated plainly
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract states a finding that would surprise an informed reader (violates a natural expectation) and states it directly, not buried in caveats. Score 0 if all findings are expected/incremental improvements in the anticipated direction.
proposals.rationale: R6 shows MLPs provably converge to linear functions and thus fail to extrapolate most nonlinear functions — a surprising negative result; R22 shows GCNs 'exponentially lose expressive power' with depth. Both carry notable dense weight (dense .532, .323) that a checklist scoring 'novelty' generically may not specifically capture.

proposals.name: Practical or societal stakes beyond technical novelty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract motivates the problem with a concrete real-world consequence (safety, fairness, cost, deployment barrier) that would matter even to a non-specialist. Score 0 if the motivation is purely 'this improves state-of-the-art on a benchmark.'
proposals.rationale: R13 (Certify or Predict) frames its contribution around the practical unusability of certified defenses due to accuracy loss; R50 (q-FFL) motivates fairness of accuracy distribution across real devices. Both score well above their card_pct on dense (R13 dense .774 vs card .887 is close, but R50 dense .581 vs card .419 shows dense crediting the stakes framing more).

proposals.name: Theory-practice bridging
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract pairs a formal/theoretical result with a matching empirical validation of that same claim. Score 0 if the abstract is purely theoretical with no empirical check, or purely empirical with no theoretical grounding for the claim made.
proposals.rationale: R6 pairs a theoretical NTK-based extrapolation analysis with matching empirical confirmation across settings; by contrast R38 and R43 are pure-theory abstracts with no empirical validation and sit at very low dense percentiles (.056, .032) despite technical density — suggesting dense discounts theory-only work more than the scorecard does (card .065, .097).

proposals.name: Accessibility of the core insight to a non-specialist expert reader
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if a reader outside the exact subfield could grasp the core idea and why it works from the abstract alone, without needing to already know the cited prior methods. Score 0 if the abstract requires familiarity with multiple named prior techniques and dense jargon to parse the contribution.
proposals.rationale: R59 (Tent) and R55 (DDPG) state their core ideas in plain terms. R16 (SSFG/MSSFG/PSSFG) and R23 (AdVIL) require the reader to already track several named priors (RAE, sliced Gromov-Wasserstein, von Mises-Fisher, contrastive divergence) — both are dense_low_card_high, suggesting jargon density may inflate card scores relative to dense.

proposals.name: Decisiveness of claim language
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if claims are stated as concrete, falsifiable results ('achieves X', 'we show Y'). Score 0 if claims are hedged with soft language ('we argue', 'we believe', 'may lead to') without a concrete demonstrated result attached.
proposals.rationale: R33 (Fidelity-Weighted Learning) leans on 'We argue that if the learner could somehow know...' hedged framing, and sits at a middling dense percentile (.435) despite reasonable card (.516); contrast with R57 and R55, which state decisive, falsifiable achievements and score very high on dense.

proposals.name: Honest scoping of a narrow setting vs. overclaimed generality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract is explicit and precise about the exact (possibly narrow) setting where the result holds, without inflating the claim beyond it. Score 0 if the abstract uses broad general language while the actual result applies only to a narrow special case, or is vague about scope.
proposals.rationale: R56 explicitly scopes its guarantee to networks 'with a single output neuron' and separately states where the method breaks down — an honest narrow claim; R34 similarly scopes to planar curves under two named transformation groups. Both show meaningfully higher dense than card (R56 dense .355 vs card .129), suggesting dense rewards precise honest scoping that a criterion-based scorecard may punish for narrowness alone.

proposals.name: Depth over breadth-padding in stated contributions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract's contribution is a single deep result explored thoroughly. Score 0 if the abstract lists many small, loosely connected add-on contributions (three named variants, several unrelated bullet points) seemingly to pad perceived contribution count.
proposals.rationale: R16 stacks a base method plus two named variants (MSSFG, PSSFG) each solving a different sub-problem, while R7 similarly tacks on 'Last, we propose a sample selection framework for...GANs' as an apparent add-on unrelated to its main PSI contribution. Both are notably weaker on dense than a focused single-idea paper like R59 or R12.

proposals.name: Foundational/first-of-kind claim with supporting evidence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly and credibly claims to be the first work to establish some capability, benchmark, or theoretical result, and supports it. Score 0 if the abstract only claims an incremental improvement over one specific prior baseline.
proposals.rationale: R45 claims to be 'the first work to prove the existence of accurate, interval-certified networks' and R37 claims CLEVER is 'the first attack-independent robustness metric' — both carry credible foundational framing. R45 lands close on both scales (dense .403/card .403), useful as a within-slice check that this factor is not merely restating outcome, while R37's larger dense_low_card_high gap (dense .613/card .742) suggests the scorecard may reward stated novelty language more heavily than dense does.

proposals.name: Abstract length / word count
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, rate how LONG this abstract is relative to a typical conference abstract (0 = a few words/title-only, 10 = maximally long and dense with clauses). Score only extent of length, not whether the length is appropriate or the writing is good.
proposals.rationale: R04 and R57 are title-only stubs (a handful of words) while R06 and R25 run to 150+ words with many clauses; length varies enormously and independently of the two models' targets, and could mechanically inflate or deflate either scorer's read of 'substance'.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice/venue norm for abstract length; how much text the mining pipeline captured

proposals.name: Code/repo release boilerplate mention
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much this abstract contains an explicit mention of released code, a GitHub link, or a project webpage (e.g. 'Code is available at...', 'alfworld.github.io'). 0 = no such mention, 10 = prominent explicit link/boilerplate. Do not judge whether releasing code is good practice.
proposals.rationale: R01 (github.com/Meituan-AutoML), R12 (github.com/yxgeee/MMT), R51 (alfworld.github.io), and R55 (github.com/Zhouaojun) all carry explicit release links while most rows do not; this is a marker of author/lab practice and resourcing that can independently sway a reader's impression.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's/lab's practice of publishing code; institutional resourcing and reputation

proposals.name: Superlative/marketing adjective density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of superlative or promotional phrasing such as 'state-of-the-art', 'novel', 'significantly', 'substantially', 'unprecedented', 'excellent performance'. 0 = plain descriptive prose, 10 = saturated with such phrasing. Score only how much such language is present, not whether the claims are true or the paper is actually strong.
proposals.rationale: R08 ('significantly improve the state-of-the-art'), R28, and R31 ('unprecedented quality') are heavy with promotional adjectives while R03 or R57 are comparatively flat; this is a stylistic habit that can move a reader's impression without tracking actual contribution.

proposals.name: Quantitative result-figure density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how many concrete numeric results (percentages, benchmark scores, counts like '34%', '8.80', '47000 experiments') appear in the text. 0 = no numbers, 10 = many numeric figures packed in. Judge only the count/density of numbers present, not whether the numbers are impressive or correct.
proposals.rationale: R09 ('34%...38%'), R30, and R48 ('47000 experiments') are dense with specific numbers while R02, R03, and R57 report none; numeric density is a salient surface cue for both a dense reader and a scorecard judge that need not track underlying quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only (also reflects how much experimental work is described in the abstract text itself)

proposals.name: Catchy named-method/acronym branding
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the title/abstract introduces a memorable coined name or acronym for the proposed method (e.g. 'DARTS-', 'DIRT-T', 'CLEVER', 'Tent', 'FWM'). 0 = no distinctive name, purely descriptive title, 10 = a strongly branded, quotable acronym/name is central. Do not judge whether the branding is deserved.
proposals.rationale: R01 (DARTS-), R08 (DIRT-T/VADA), R49 (CLEVER), and R23 (Tent) all foreground a catchy coined name, versus purely descriptive titles like R36 ('Understanding image motion with group representations') or R60; branding is a stylistic practice that can independently drive memorability/impression.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's marketing savvy / practice of branding methods, often correlated with lab experience in this exact venue format

proposals.name: Explicit novelty-priority claim ('first to...')
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how explicitly the abstract stakes a priority claim such as 'first to', 'for the first time', 'to the best of our knowledge, this is the first'. 0 = no such claim, 10 = prominent, repeated priority claims. Score only the presence of the claim language, not whether the claim is actually true or important.
proposals.rationale: R24 ('this is the first work to prove...'), R43 ('we are the first to obtain'), and R45 hedge with priority language, while most other rows make no such claim; this phrasing is partly a rhetorical habit tied to how contested/crowded the sub-topic already is, independent of actual novelty.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the submission/topic stream — whether the authors believe they are staking early ground in a crowded sub-area

proposals.name: Title-only / truncated-abstract artifact
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much this entry consists only of a title (and possibly a one-line fragment like 'International audience') with no substantive abstract body. 0 = full abstract present, 10 = title/stub only with essentially no body text. This is a mechanical completeness check, not a quality judgement.
proposals.rationale: R04 ('Distributional Concavity Regularization for GANs' — title only) and R57 ('International audience' with no real abstract) are missing-text artifacts of data collection, not signals about the underlying paper's quality, yet a scorecard built on criterion text would likely score both near-zero on everything for lack of material.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only (artifact of the corpus scraping/mining pipeline)

proposals.name: Epistemic hedging language density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the density of tentative/hedging phrases such as 'we conjecture', 'we argue', 'we believe', 'we hypothesize', 'we speculate'. 0 = no hedging, confident declarative claims throughout, 10 = heavy reliance on such hedges. Score only how much hedging language appears, not whether hedging is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('we conjecture that skip connections...') and R44 ('we argue that the improved accuracy...') lean on hedged claims, whereas empirical papers like R09 or R30 state results as fact; this stylistic register tracks subfield culture and authorial caution more than the underlying finding's soundness.
proposals.upstream_parent: subfield/venue norm for theoretical caution, and possibly submission timing (rushed/incomplete theoretical work hedges more)

proposals.name: Inline named prior-work citation density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how many explicit inline citations to specific prior authors/years appear in the abstract text itself (e.g. '(Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015)', '(Trouillon et al., 2016)', '(Downey et al.)'). 0 = no named citations, 10 = several named citations woven into the prose. Score only the count/presence of such citations, not the appropriateness of the comparison.
proposals.rationale: R08, R16, and R60 pepper the abstract with named inline citations signaling deep familiarity with a specific lineage of prior work, while R02, R30, or R33 cite no one by name in the abstract; this is partly a marker of an author's standing/practice in the sub-community rather than the work's own merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's embeddedness/seniority in the specific sub-literature; degree of engagement with 'insider' framing common to veteran authors in this format

proposals.name: Framed-as-response-to-recent-work positioning
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract frames its contribution explicitly as addressing a gap, weakness, or limitation in a 'recent' or 'existing' method/approach (e.g. 'a recent attempt...has a weakness', 'existing approaches...however', 'despite promising, state-of-the-art results...are far from satisfactory'). 0 = frames itself as opening a new problem with no reference to a recent predecessor's shortcomings, 10 = explicitly and prominently positioned as a corrective response to a specific recent prior method. Do not judge whether the criticism of prior work is fair or the fix is good.
proposals.rationale: R06 ('a recent attempt...has a weakness since it treats every slicing direction similarly') and R24 ('while promising, state-of-the-art results...are far from satisfactory') read as late-arriving, corrective riffs on an already-established recent method, versus R33 or R11 which read as foundational/early entries in their sub-area; this positioning fingerprint tracks where in the topic's lifecycle the abstract was written, not the quality of the fix itself.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the run of submissions on this sub-topic — how late-arriving/derivative the work is relative to when the topic became active, i.e. whether the authors had already seen the 'obvious' first takes

proposals.name: Mechanistic Diagnosis and Remedy
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a specific failure mechanism, derives the intervention from it, and explains the expected correction; score 0 when the method is an unexplained bundle or generic tweak.
proposals.rationale: R29, R34, R35, and R41 explicitly connect observed limitations to proposed mechanisms, unlike abstracts relying mainly on method novelty or benchmark claims.

proposals.name: Causal Isolation of Contributions
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract describes controlled comparisons or ablations that isolate each component's contribution; score 0 when several changes are introduced together without any stated way to distinguish them.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R04 separate the roles of multiple design choices, while R45 and R54 motivate several interacting modifications whose individual roles require especially careful isolation.

proposals.name: Theory-to-Algorithm Closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal assumptions, theoretical claims, and the implemented algorithm are explicitly connected; score 0 when theory is ornamental, disconnected from the method, or unsupported by stated conditions.
proposals.rationale: R10, R18, R42, and R56 tightly connect mathematical conditions to concrete algorithms or guarantees, a dimension not captured by generic novelty descriptions.

proposals.name: Structural Inductive-Bias Fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the architecture or objective encodes a regularity central to the task and the abstract explains why that structure fits; score 0 when a generic architecture is applied without task-specific structure.
proposals.rationale: R07, R16, R48, and R49 use embodiment, chemistry, algorithmic structure, or hierarchy as explicit modeling biases rather than merely adding capacity.

proposals.name: Cross-Level Interface Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies how representations or processes at distinct abstraction levels exchange information through a clear interface; score 0 when integration is asserted only as end-to-end learning or modularity.
proposals.rationale: R07 links text-level plans to visual actions, R52 links tables with text, and R60 links latent parallel sequences with observed styles.

proposals.name: Stress-Test Alignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when evaluation settings directly instantiate the method's anticipated failure modes or distribution shifts using several controlled stressors; score 0 when evaluation is limited to routine in-distribution benchmarks.
proposals.rationale: R08, R11, R22, and R41 evaluate transfer, perturbation, domain, or extrapolation behavior that directly matches the stated motivation.

proposals.name: Task-Bottleneck Centrality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the work targets a clearly task-defining bottleneck that limits existing approaches and changes that bottleneck directly; score 0 when it mainly offers a minor convenience or cosmetic metric change.
proposals.rationale: R10 addresses feature cost in predictive-state models, R31 addresses costly privileged information, R52 addresses cross-source evidence retrieval, and R54 addresses pseudo-label noise.

proposals.name: Conceptual Unification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the framework derives explicit relationships among previously separate methods and presents them as one coherent formulation; score 0 when related techniques are merely juxtaposed under a new name.
proposals.rationale: R46, R53, R60, and R22 each connect multiple established perspectives through a shared formulation or explanatory framework.

proposals.name: Assumption and Boundary Transparency
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract states applicability assumptions, limiting conditions, and plausible failure cases; score 0 when it makes broad claims without specifying where they may fail.
proposals.rationale: R11, R14, R18, and R57 explicitly discuss representational, attack, sample-size, or output-dimension limits instead of presenting unrestricted claims.

proposals.name: Tradeoff Articulation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract names competing objectives, explains their tension, and describes how the method controls both; score 0 when it presents only one metric or vaguely claims simultaneous improvement.
proposals.rationale: R01, R12, R23, and R39 make accuracy, uncertainty, robustness, compression, or precision tradeoffs explicit.

proposals.name: Constraint-Native Practicality
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when real constraints such as latency, memory, labels, communication, or information access shape the method and are addressed concretely; score 0 when practicality appears only as an adjective.
proposals.rationale: R01, R31, R37, and R43 build latency, privileged-information access, training cost, or hardware efficiency into the design problem.

proposals.name: Diagnostic Evaluation Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when experiments are structured to distinguish mechanism, scope, and alternatives through matched baselines, ablations, and varied conditions; score 0 when the abstract offers only a single benchmark comparison.
proposals.rationale: R03, R04, R40, and R45 emphasize controlled comparisons, large evaluation frameworks, or component-specific analysis rather than one headline number.

proposals.name: Evidence-Bearing Specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when each major claim is paired with concrete tasks, data regimes, comparisons, metrics, and conditions; score 0 when the abstract relies mainly on superlatives, benchmark names, or generic assertions.
proposals.rationale: R15, R25, R38, and R54 contain many numerical or procedural claims, making specificity a useful discriminator from broad promotional language.

proposals.name: Reproduction Readiness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies code, data, videos, protocols, or implementation details sufficient to support independent reproduction; score 0 when neither resources nor reproducibility-relevant detail is provided.
proposals.rationale: R07, R29, R37, and R40 explicitly emphasize code, data, videos, or controlled protocols, whereas many abstracts provide only conceptual descriptions.

proposals.name: Reusable Abstraction Level
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the central idea is stated at a level that naturally maps across tasks or domains and the abstract explains those mappings; score 0 when the contribution is inseparable from one benchmark and has no reusable abstraction.
proposals.rationale: R05, R28, R36, and R58 formulate broadly reusable ideas about topology, invariance, dynamic graphs, or embeddings rather than narrow task-specific tricks.

proposals.name: Branded method naming
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract use coined acronyms, branded method names, or playful titles? Judge only visible naming, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Memorable naming is an attention and recognition shortcut unrelated to research quality. Examples include FBS in R02, CLEVER in R15, and DARTS- in R40.

proposals.name: Prior-work name density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract foreground named authors, papers, systems, or explicit comparative lineage? Judge only visible citation-style density, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Authors' conventions for signaling literature familiarity can be mistaken for substance, while also reflecting genuine scholarly competence. R10 names PSRNNs, ORFs, and Kernel Bayes Rule; R25 names multiple Go systems and prior papers.

proposals.name: Copyediting regularity
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much is the prose grammatically polished, typographically consistent, and free of obvious editing artifacts? Judge only surface regularity, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Editing resources leave visible traces that can act as nuisance proxies without changing the underlying research. R20 contains 'unstruc-tured' and 'modelcan', while R25 contains HTML artifacts and inconsistent system names.

proposals.name: Abstract length and detail
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much textual length and procedural detail does the abstract contain? Judge only amount of text and detail, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Available space, author preference, or submission conventions can make verbosity predictive while being unrelated to quality. R06 and R10 are highly elaborated, whereas R12 is only a title-like fragment and R54 is nearly empty.

proposals.name: Quantified result density
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract include exact numerical gains, benchmark values, resource savings, or named performance thresholds? Judge only quantity of numerical reporting, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Competitive presentation norms can reward easily extracted numbers even when reporting density is not research quality. R07 gives BLEU values and latency claims; R21 lists several exact mAP gains; R41 reports multiple bit-width results.

proposals.name: Fashionable topic vocabulary
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract use terminology associated with currently prominent ML themes or application agendas? Judge only topical vocabulary, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Community attention can make certain terms unusually salient to text-based systems without making the underlying work better. R15 and R45 emphasize adversarial or certified robustness, while R57 emphasizes causality, robustness, and out-of-distribution generalization.

proposals.name: Temporal and version markers
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract contain dated benchmarks, named annual events, software versions, or other era-specific identifiers? Judge only visible temporal markers, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Submission era and timing leave textual fingerprints through datasets, competitions, and version labels that can become shortcuts. R07 names IWSLT 2016 and WMT 2016; R25 names a January KGS tournament; R27 names NIPS 2017.

proposals.name: Artifact and project signaling
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract advertise code, data, videos, websites, project names, or public implementation artifacts? Judge only visible artifact signaling, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Public-project habits can influence discoverability independently of research quality, while also plausibly correlating with reproducibility practices. R21 and R40 include code links, and R44 advertises code, data, videos, and a project website.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's dissemination practice and audience visibility

proposals.name: Canonical-template framing
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract follow a familiar, canonical problem-template sequence of motivation, standard gap, method, benchmark, and expected application? Judge only rhetorical structure, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: An entry's position in a crowded stream could influence whether it adopts an obvious early framing or a later corrective framing; that position is invisible except through textual style. R01 and R32 use highly canonical problem-to-method framing, while R40 foregrounds a specific corrective to an established failure mode.

proposals.name: Priority and superlative rhetoric
proposals.instruction: On a 0-10 scale, how much does the abstract use priority, novelty, superiority, record, or unusually strong self-promotional wording? Judge only presence of such rhetoric, not whether the work is good.
proposals.rationale: Persuasive style can be learned as a shortcut despite not measuring research quality. R22 says 'first work' and 'arbitrarily close'; R48 claims 'unprecedented quality' and a 'record' score; R39 describes 'superior performance'.

proposals.name: Mechanistic bottleneck-to-method fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract identifies a concrete failure mechanism and an intervention that directly addresses it; score 0 when it merely pairs a generic problem with a generic method.
proposals.rationale: R12 explains architecture-search collapse through privileged skip connections and targets that mechanism. R24 diagnoses weak perturbations from local curvature and designs defenses around that failure.

proposals.name: Theory-to-algorithm closure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when formal analysis directly determines the algorithm, assumptions, or design choices; score 0 when theory is ornamental and disconnected from the proposed method.
proposals.rationale: R07 turns provable feedback-alignment guarantees into a learning algorithm. R17 extends random-feature theory specifically to justify the proposed recurrent architecture.

proposals.name: Boundary-condition characterization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly states when the method works, fails, or changes behavior, including relevant data or parameter conditions; score 0 when it makes unqualified claims.
proposals.rationale: R47 gives explicit sample-size thresholds for descent-path guarantees. R53 distinguishes extrapolation behavior by target-function structure and training-distribution diversity.

proposals.name: Resource-fidelity tradeoff design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when resource savings are precisely defined and the method explains how task-relevant fidelity is preserved; score 0 when efficiency is asserted without a concrete mechanism or accounting.
proposals.rationale: R03 removes whole filters to obtain hardware-compatible computation savings. R15 explicitly trades parallel decoding latency against translation fidelity through identifiable training mechanisms.

proposals.name: Structural invariance preservation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the method explicitly encodes symmetries, physical constraints, or nuisance invariances and explains how they shape learned representations; score 0 when structure is only mentioned as motivation.
proposals.rationale: R02 builds geometric invariants for transformations, noise, sampling, and occlusion. R37 encodes atom conservation and reaction sparsity through electron-path prediction.

proposals.name: Cross-level interface coherence
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract defines coherent interfaces between abstract representations and concrete observations, actions, or outputs; score 0 when its stages are disconnected or underspecified.
proposals.rationale: R04 links textual planning to visually grounded embodied actions through a shared pipeline. R58 explicitly connects heterogeneous table and text evidence through retrieval and reading interfaces.

proposals.name: Compositional modular reuse
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when components have explicit interfaces and can be recombined across models, tasks, or settings; score 0 when the proposal is an inseparable one-off system.
proposals.rationale: R04 presents modular language, planning, navigation, and perception components. R33 describes a compositional architecture that combines certified and high-accuracy networks.

proposals.name: Meaningful latent structure
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when latent variables correspond to interpretable factors or reusable operations and the abstract explains how they affect observable behavior; score 0 when latent representations are opaque placeholders.
proposals.rationale: R28 stores compositional associations in a rapidly changing memory for novel relational inference. R59 learns ordered subtask structure and recovers boundaries in demonstrations.

proposals.name: Component-level causal attribution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract isolates how individual design choices contribute through controlled comparisons or staged analysis; score 0 when many changes are bundled without attribution.
proposals.rationale: R08 traces the roles of probabilistic modeling, latent alignment, and variational inference in a unified formulation. R30 explicitly examines pruning at initialization and compares its gradient-preservation criterion with alternatives.

proposals.name: Principled cross-regime generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when variation across domains, tasks, scales, or environments is motivated by the proposed mechanism; score 0 when breadth consists only of unrelated applications.
proposals.rationale: R31 connects inverse-reinforcement learning to changing dynamics and structures through empowerment regularization. R43 links augmentation invariance to both distribution shift and varied sequential decision tasks.

proposals.name: Validity of robustness evaluation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the threat model, perturbation protocol, metric, and claimed robustness notion are aligned and their limitations are acknowledged; score 0 when robustness relies on a weak or mismatched proxy.
proposals.rationale: R35 defines an attack-agnostic robustness metric through local Lipschitz analysis and extreme-value theory. R24 distinguishes weak single-step perturbations from transferred and randomized attacks.

proposals.name: Scope of guarantees and uncertainty
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract clearly distinguishes formal guarantees, predictive uncertainty, and empirical behavior and states each one's scope; score 0 when such terms are used without qualification.
proposals.rationale: R13 precisely states an approximation and interval-certification existence guarantee. R40 separates posterior uncertainty over quantized parameters from predictive calibration.

proposals.name: Information-access accounting
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract specifies which labels, privileged inputs, or supervision signals are available at each stage and how access is reduced; score 0 when low-supervision claims leave information access ambiguous.
proposals.rationale: R41 specifies that privileged information is accessed selectively based only on standard observations. R25 distinguishes trusted labels, weak labels, and teacher access in its training procedure.

proposals.name: Conceptual unification
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the proposal derives meaningful relationships among previously separate methods or objectives within one framework; score 0 when it merely places familiar techniques side by side.
proposals.rationale: R08 unifies generative and non-generative style-transfer objectives through a latent probabilistic formulation. R22 derives several associative-memory models from a common microscopic theory.

proposals.name: Claim auditability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the abstract gives precise contributions, settings, procedures, scope, and reproducibility details that let a reader audit its claims; score 0 when it is mostly a title, slogan, or unsupported general assertion.
proposals.rationale: R23 specifies a controlled evaluation framework, many experiments, model classes, and datasets. R04 supplies a concrete simulator, agent decomposition, and code, data, and video artifacts, whereas R20 and R48 provide almost no auditable detail.

proposals.name: Verbosity and claim packing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much prose, subordinate clauses, and distinct contribution or result claims are packed into the abstract; judge only extent, not whether the claims are good or high quality.
proposals.rationale: Dense claim packing can influence attention and text representation without evidencing research quality. R04 and R36 contain many sequential claims, tasks, and comparisons.

proposals.name: Formal notation density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent of displayed mathematics, symbolic notation, theorem-style language, and technical formalism; judge only extent, not whether the formalism is correct or valuable.
proposals.rationale: Mathematical typography can create a recognizable processing cue independent of research quality. R20 and R54 contain unusually dense formal and optimization notation.

proposals.name: Acronym and name density
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract introduces capitalized method, model, dataset, or loss names and acronym expansions; judge only naming prevalence, not whether the names are useful.
proposals.rationale: Brand-like naming can affect memorability and textual salience without being evidence of quality. R02 introduces MMT and multiple named losses, while R07 introduces SSFG, MSSFG, and PSSFG.

proposals.name: Citation-lineage anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent of explicit citations, named predecessors, canonical methods, and lineage comparisons; judge only visible anchoring, not the importance or correctness of the cited work.
proposals.rationale: Authors embedded in a visible research lineage may cite recognizable predecessors in ways that shape reader priors, while citation density itself is not quality. R04 names several prior Go systems, and R48 anchors its framing in domain-adversarial training and the cluster assumption.

proposals.name: Benchmark-result numerics
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract foregrounds exact percentages, ranks, dataset counts, metric values, rollout counts, or leaderboard-style comparisons; judge only numerical density, not whether the numbers are impressive.
proposals.rationale: Numerical specificity is a strong genre cue that can influence text processing without itself establishing quality. R02 lists multiple exact mAP improvements, while R38 gives several bit-width and accuracy figures.

proposals.name: Promotional certainty language
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent of superlatives and assertive promotional phrases such as “first,” “state-of-the-art,” “unprecedented,” “excellent,” or “substantial”; judge only phrase prevalence, not whether the claims are justified.
proposals.rationale: Booster language can alter perceived salience independently of research quality. R39 uses “unprecedented quality” and “record” language, while R50 uses “first,” “novel,” and strong alignment claims.

proposals.name: Artifact availability signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract advertises code, data, videos, project pages, repositories, or other immediately accessible artifacts; judge only the presence and prominence of these signals, not their usefulness.
proposals.rationale: Artifact signaling can affect reader priors while being distinct from the underlying research quality. R02 provides a GitHub link, and R05 provides code, data, videos, and a project website.

proposals.name: Editorial irregularity
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent of typos, malformed grammar, encoding artifacts, sentence fragments, spacing problems, or visibly inconsistent terminology; judge only textual irregularity, not the author's competence or research quality.
proposals.rationale: Surface editing artifacts can change readability and model representation without constituting research evidence. R11 contains forms such as “unstruc-tured” and “modelcan,” while R33 contains the spelling “Eucledian” and R26 is only a fragment.

proposals.name: Era-marked terminology
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 the extent to which the abstract contains period-specific benchmarks, older model families, dated citations, or language signaling a particular research era; judge only temporal cues, not whether the work is current or valuable.
proposals.rationale: Temporal vocabulary can act as a corpus-position cue without being research quality. R04 cites 2015–2016 Go systems and KGS-era comparisons, while R34 contrasts DNNs with GMMs and shallow networks in an older speech-recognition framing.

proposals.name: Canonical versus late-riff framing
proposals.instruction: Rate 0-10 how much the abstract reads as a canonical, immediately recognizable treatment of a familiar prompt rather than a highly specific recombination of an already crowded topic; score only this textual impression, do not infer actual submission order, and do not judge quality.
proposals.rationale: An entry's apparent canonicality or late-riff character can reflect where it sits in a crowded stream, while neither textual style establishes quality. R27 uses a highly familiar continuous-control framing, whereas R46 and R60 present more specialized recombinations around electron paths and microscopic associative memory.

proposals.name: Paradigm-Challenging Premise Together with Rigorous Justification
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract purely follows standard assumptions without questioning them, or makes contrarian claims without support. Score 10 if it explicitly identifies a fundamental, widely-held assumption in the field and provides rigorous theoretical or empirical proof that it is wrong or unnecessary.
proposals.rationale: The dense model likely rewards highly impactful, assumption-breaking work that a rigid scorecard might penalize for not following standard problem formulations. R09 and R18 are excellent examples of dense_high_card_low abstracts that directly challenge fundamental field norms (the necessity of normalization, and the universal approximation of skinny networks).

proposals.name: Mechanistic Explanation Together with Actionable Solution
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract proposes an empirical trick or algorithm without explaining the underlying mechanics. Score 10 if it pairs a deep conceptual model explaining exactly *why* a phenomenon or failure mode occurs with a concrete algorithm designed specifically to exploit that mechanism.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard might miss the elegance of diagnosing an underlying mechanism. R07 (diagnosing and fixing DARTS performance collapse) and R49 (identifying small curvature artifacts in adversarial training and proposing a targeted fix) exemplify this high-level research quality that the dense model favors.

proposals.name: Conceptual Unification Together with Broad Generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract introduces a niche, standalone method. Score 10 if it presents a general theoretical framework that mathematically or conceptually subsumes multiple previously distinct state-of-the-art methods into a single coherent paradigm.
proposals.rationale: Papers that unify disjoint fields or methods demonstrate high research maturity. R38 (deriving modern Hopfield networks from a biological microscopic theory) and R54 (unifying VAEs and autoregressive models into a principled lossy framework) represent the kind of deep, unifying quality the dense model detects beyond basic scorecard checkboxes.

proposals.name: Fine-Grained Failure Analysis Together with Targeted Mitigation
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract vaguely claims prior work is 'suboptimal' or 'slow'. Score 10 if it pinpoints the exact mathematical, architectural, or structural bottleneck of prior methods and proposes a solution specifically architected to bypass that exact bottleneck.
proposals.rationale: R03 (identifying the exact limitations of feature distribution matching in domain adversarial training) and R57 (characterizing the exact asymptotic information loss in GNNs) illustrate the precise diagnostic quality that elevates a paper in the eyes of an end-to-end dense model.

proposals.name: Lexical Economy Together with High Conceptual Density
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the text is cluttered with dense acronyms, hyper-specific jargon, and buzzwords that obscure the core idea. Score 10 if it uses plain, precise language with zero unnecessary jargon while conveying deep, complex conceptual content.
proposals.rationale: A scorecard model built on explicit keyword banks is easily fooled by buzzword-heavy text. The dense model heavily favors elegant plain language in dense_high_card_low abstracts like R55 and R54, while penalizing dense_low_card_high abstracts like R34 and R59 that overuse complex-sounding but low-substance terminology.

proposals.name: Novel Problem Formulation Together with Infrastructure
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract tackles a heavily studied, standard benchmark task. Score 10 if it formalizes a completely new problem space that connects previously disjoint domains, and provides the necessary infrastructure (datasets, simulators) to explore it.
proposals.rationale: Proposing a new problem is often more valuable than an incremental solution to an old one. proposals.name: Theoretical Characterization Together with Expressivity Bounds

proposals.name: Interdisciplinary Foundation Together with Structural Mapping

proposals.name: Abstract Reasoning Together with Low-Level Execution

R19 (using Fast Weight Memory to perform associative compositional inference) and R41 (executing multi-hop reasoning across tables and unstructured text) demonstrate this property.

proposals.name: Broad Applicability Together with Minimal Architectural Overhead
