proposals.rationale: R09 (Fixup initialization allowing any residual network to train without normalization) and R55 (filter pruning applicable to standard VGG/ResNets using existing dense libraries) represent the kind of elegantly general contributions that scorecards often miss but dense models highly rate.

proposals.name: Structural Inductive Bias Together with Emergent Unsupervised Learning
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the model uses generic function approximation relying entirely on massive supervised labels. Score 10 if it embeds a specific structural or hierarchical constraint into the architecture that allows complex latent structures to emerge without explicit supervision.
proposals.rationale: R02 (using Ordered Memory Policy Networks to let subtask hierarchies emerge from unstructured demonstrations) and R14 (using hierarchical multiscale RNNs to capture latent sequence structures without explicit boundary information) exemplify this sophisticated learning paradigm.

proposals.name: Nuanced Empirical Positioning Together with Honest Baselines
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract makes sweeping, unqualified claims of 'state-of-the-art' performance. Score 10 if it carefully bounds its empirical claims, transparently provides baseline metrics to establish task difficulty, and explicitly acknowledges where the method might fail.
proposals.rationale: An end-to-end model values intellectual honesty and transparency, whereas a scorecard might just look for the phrase 'state-of-the-art'. R49 (transparently acknowledging that subsequent elaborate attacks reduced their model's accuracy) and R41 (providing explicit baselines below 10% to honestly frame the task difficulty) anchor this criterion.

proposals.name: Mechanism Simplification Together with Practical Scaling
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract introduces increasingly convoluted mechanisms to achieve marginal gains. Score 10 if it proposes a minimalist, highly elegant solution that drastically reduces system complexity while maintaining or improving scaling properties.
proposals.rationale: The dense model recognizes when a complex problem is solved with beautiful simplicity. R55 (replacing complex sparse pruning with simple whole-filter pruning to accelerate CNNs easily) and R54 (using a simple principled combination of VAEs and autoregressive models for lossy representations) showcase this elegance.

proposals.name: Causal Inference Together with Invariance Enforcement
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract optimizes purely for exploiting surface-level statistical correlations in the data. Score 10 if it explicitly models the underlying causal data-generating process or structural constraints to enforce out-of-distribution invariance.
proposals.rationale: The dense model is capable of perceiving the conceptual depth of causal modeling beyond just seeing the word 'causal'. R47 (analyzing neural network extrapolation through the lens of underlying non-linearities and diverse training distributions) and R46 (using group properties to structurally enforce motion invariance) are prime examples.

proposals.name: Fine-Grained Efficiency Together with Deployment Readiness
proposals.instruction: Score 0 if the abstract achieves theoretical or marginal empirical gains without real-world practical viability. Score 10 if it proposes a method explicitly optimizing for memory, latency, or compute at a granular level (e.g., dynamic execution, low-precision math) that is directly deployable on standard hardware.
proposals.rationale: R37 (predictively skipping unimportant convolutional channels at runtime to accelerate execution dynamically) and R05 (converting pre-trained weights to low-precision powers-of-two for highly efficient deployment) show a practical focus that the dense model evaluates favorably against purely theoretical efficiency claims.

proposals.name: Branded System or Acronym Prominence
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract explicitly introduces, capitalizes, or heavily uses a specific acronym, system name, or branded method (e.g., ALFWorld, DARTS-, MMT). Do not judge whether the name is good or creative.
proposals.rationale: Prominently branding a method is a marketing or formatting habit that a scorecard model might mistakenly reward as a 'clear contribution', whereas the dense model evaluates the text organically. E.g., R05 introduces ALFWorld/BUTLER, R12 names DARTS-, and R38 introduces MMT.

proposals.name: Explicit Code or Resource Link
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract includes an explicit URL, Github link, or statement about code/data availability. Do not judge the usefulness or validity of the link.
proposals.rationale: Providing links in the abstract reflects an author's formatting convention or established lab practice rather than the core research quality of the text itself, though scorecard models often give points for 'reproducibility'. E.g., R05 provides a project page, R12 includes a Github link, and R38 links to their code.

proposals.name: Raw Numerical Metric Reporting
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract explicitly cites specific quantitative performance metrics, speedups, or numerical scores (e.g., '5x savings', '14.4% mAP'). Do not judge whether the metrics are impressive.
proposals.rationale: Dumping exact numbers is a writing style choice often rewarded by scorecards checking for 'empirical evidence' boxes. E.g., R21 reports '5x and 2x savings', R38 lists '14.4%, 18.2%' improvements, and R56 states a record inception score of '8.80'.

proposals.name: Mathematical Notation Density
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text contains raw LaTeX formatting, inline math symbols, or mathematical notation (e.g., $x$, \emph{}, l_\infty). Do not judge the correctness of the math.
proposals.rationale: Heavy use of raw math notation indicates a theoretical focus or a failure to convert to plain text, which might trick a scorecard judge into scoring higher for 'technical rigor'. E.g., R17 uses inline math for variables, R40 discusses estimators with symbols, and R58 includes perturbation notation.

proposals.name: Metadata Artifacts and Typos
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract contains obvious metadata artifacts, formatting glitches, or unedited typos (e.g., missing spaces like 'modelcan', hyphens like 'unstruc-tured'). Do not judge if this makes the paper bad.
proposals.rationale: Artifacts like these indicate upstream factors like rushed submission preparation or poor PDF-to-text extraction pipelines. E.g., R04 contains 'unstruc-tured' and 'modelcan', while R15 literally just says 'International audience' as its abstract.

proposals.name: Corporate or Competition Signaling
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text references specific external servers, well-known corporate affiliations, or formal competitions. Do not judge the prestige of the references.
proposals.rationale: Explicitly referencing competitions or corporate GitHub names reflects upstream institutional backing rather than intrinsic research quality. E.g., R12 names 'Meituan-AutoML', R16 references the 'NIPS 2017 competition', and R22 cites the 'KGS Go Server'.

proposals.name: Broad Philosophical or Hype Framing
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract uses expansive, broad philosophical framing or appeals to human abilities (e.g., 'human intelligence', 'ancient game'). Do not judge whether the framing is appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Using grandiose framing is an upstream authorial practice aimed at social audience appeal, potentially inflating scorecard scores for 'significance' without reflecting dense technical value. E.g., R14 calls math a 'core ability within human intelligence', R22 describes Go as a 'long-term goal of artificial intelligence', and R31 mentions 'long-standing challenges'.

proposals.name: Explicit Inline Citation Syntax
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text contains explicit inline citations or author references using parenthetical syntax (e.g., '(Author et al., Year)'). Do not judge if the citations are appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Explicit citations in abstracts are often unnecessary and reflect an author's local writing style or venue template, which a scorecard might incorrectly associate with 'literature contextualization'. E.g., R05 includes '(Cote et al., 2018)', R18 cites '(Trouillon et al., 2016)', and R60 cites '(Ganin & Lempitsky, 2015)'.

proposals.name: Reactive Positioning to Prior Work
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the abstract explicitly frames itself as fixing, relieving, or responding to 'existing methods', 'previous works', or 'recent attempts'. Do not judge if the response is valid.
proposals.rationale: Reactive phrasing signals a late position in the entry stream—a riff on established work—which scorecards often reward for 'addressing a known problem' while dense models evaluate the standalone contribution. E.g., R08 opens with 'To relieve your headache of...', R12 begins 'Despite the fast development...', and R30 states 'While existing approaches...'.

proposals.name: Enumerated Contribution Lists
proposals.instruction: Rate the extent to which the text uses explicit bullet-point style or enumerated lists of contributions (e.g., 'Our contributions are three-fold: (i)... (ii)...'). Do not judge the clarity of the list.
proposals.rationale: Explicitly enumerating contributions is a formatting habit from paper templates that scorecard models might heavily weight as a 'clear contribution statement', whereas dense models process the text organically. E.g., R11 lists benefits as '(a)... (b)... (c)...', R17 explicitly lists '(i)... (ii)... (iii)...', and R45 introduces 'The first variant... The second variant...'.

proposals.name: Identifies Root Cause Over Symptoms
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly identifies the fundamental mathematical or algorithmic root cause of a known failure mode and directly targets it; score 0 if it merely proposes a new architecture or loss function to alleviate a symptom without explaining why the failure happens.
proposals.rationale: The dense model appears to heavily reward deep mechanistic understanding, whereas the scorecard may miss this nuance. For example, R44 explicitly diagnoses the skip connection dominance issue in DARTS, and R58 identifies the degenerate global minimum caused by linear approximations in adversarial training, both of which the dense model rates highly.

proposals.name: Elegant Simplicity and Broad Applicability
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the proposed method is conceptually simple, requires minimal modification to existing pipelines, and acts as a drop-in replacement for standard architectures; score 0 if the method requires highly complex, bespoke hyperparameter tuning or an entirely new ecosystem to function.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly values papers that provide simple, universal solutions (e.g., R11's straightforward filter pruning, R35's simple rescaling for Fixup initialization). These are foundational contributions that a scorecard might under-credit if it focuses too heavily on complex methodological step-counts.

proposals.name: Paradigm-Shifting Challenge to Dogma
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the paper successfully challenges a widely held assumption or standard practice in the field (e.g., 'normalization is strictly necessary') and proves it is not required; score 0 if it simply iterates on the current dominant paradigm.
proposals.rationale: The dense model assigns very high percentiles to papers that fundamentally shift perspectives, such as R35 challenging the necessity of normalization layers, and R21 challenging the autoregressive bottleneck in sequence generation. The dense model perceives this conceptual boldness as a strong marker of quality.

proposals.name: Insight Extraction Over Experimental Scale
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract focuses on a deep, generalizable mechanistic insight extracted from experiments; score 0 if it substitutes brute-force scale or the sheer volume of experiments (e.g., running 47,000 experiments) for conceptual breakthrough.
proposals.rationale: The dense model penalizes abstracts that boast about experimental volume without profound takeaways (R02 is dense_low_card_high), while it highly rewards abstracts that provide compact, elegant theoretical insights (R51). The scorecard seems overly impressed by mentions of 'large-scale uniform frameworks'.

proposals.name: Theory-Guided Empirical Design
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if formal mathematical or statistical results are explicitly used to inform, design, or explain the empirical model's architecture or objective function; score 0 if theory and empirical methods are disjointed or if the method is entirely a heuristic black box.
proposals.rationale: The dense model strongly favors papers where formal theory directly shapes the algorithm (e.g., R22 provides provable guarantees for feedback alignment, and R51 links extrapolation theory to GNN architecture design). This tight coupling of theory and practice is a hallmark of high research quality that a rigid scorecard might miss.

proposals.name: Precise Characterization of Failure Modes
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract precisely articulates the exact mathematical or structural condition under which prior models fail (e.g., exponential loss of expressive power); score 0 if it vaguely states 'previous methods are suboptimal' or relies on general claims of poor performance.
proposals.rationale: Explaining exactly why things fail is highly valued by the dense model. R18 characterizes the asymptotic information loss in GCNs via graph spectra, and R58 mathematically characterizes the obfuscation caused by small curvature artifacts. The dense model credits this diagnostic precision.

proposals.name: Conceptual Unification of Disparate Methods
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract introduces a theoretical framework that subsumes or unifies previously distinct, competing approaches into a single coherent paradigm; score 0 if it introduces yet another isolated point solution to an existing array of methods.
proposals.rationale: The dense model rewards high-level theoretical synthesis. R57 unifies various modern Hopfield network models into a single microscopic theory, and R10 unifies VAEs with autoregressive models in a principled way. The scorecard may under-credit these grand unifications because their surface features look standard.

proposals.name: Lexical Clarity and Meaningful Jargon
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract uses technical terminology precisely to convey complex concepts clearly and intuitively; score 0 if it strings together dense, obscure buzzwords (e.g., 'spherical sliced fused Gromov-Wasserstein') in a way that obscures the core intuition.
proposals.rationale: The dense model reads text end-to-end and likely punishes obfuscatory jargon that signals incremental or low-impact work (R47 is dense_low_card_high, drowning in complex jargon). Conversely, it rewards crystal clear conceptual arguments (R35, R11) that a scorecard of explicit surface features might fail to appreciate.

proposals.name: Encoding of Structural Inductive Biases
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method explicitly and mathematically encodes known physical, geometric, or topological constraints into the model's architecture or objective function; score 0 for generic, black-box function approximators applied blindly to structured data.
proposals.rationale: The dense model highly rewards models that respect the inherent structure of their domains, such as R29's encoding of invariant geometric functions for planar curves, and R09's alignment of abstract text with concrete physical environments. The scorecard may not fully grasp the value of this structural matching.

proposals.name: Explicit Out-of-Distribution Generalization
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly evaluates or guarantees the model's ability to generalize to unseen data distributions, larger scales, or extrapolated domains; score 0 if it only focuses on narrow, in-distribution test set performance.
proposals.rationale: High-quality ML research focuses heavily on OOD robustness. The dense model favors papers like R51 (studying extrapolation explicitly) and R05 (addressing domain adaptation via the cluster assumption). The scorecard might over-credit standard in-distribution benchmark wins seen in other abstracts.

proposals.name: Introduction of Unifying, Falsifiable Metrics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract proposes a new, mathematically grounded or carefully constructed evaluation metric/benchmark that exposes true model capabilities and avoids Goodhart's law; score 0 if it relies entirely on standard, potentially saturated metrics.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values abstracts that change how we evaluate, provided they are rigorous (e.g., R17 proposes a new metric for GAN variation, and R50 introduces a challenging multi-hop QA dataset that exposes baseline failures). A scorecard might miss the importance of these new measurement tools.

proposals.name: Biological or Cognitive Plausibility
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract draws justified, formal connections between artificial networks and neurobiological mechanisms or cognitive science (e.g., modeling associative memory); score 0 for purely engineering-focused deep learning scaling without cognitive parallels.
proposals.rationale: The dense model places high value on interdisciplinary connections to neuroscience or cognitive science. R57 establishes a biologically plausible microscopic theory for associative memory, and R38 models human associative inference using fast weight memory. These conceptual bridges are strong quality signals.

proposals.name: Non-Trivial Trade-off Resolution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method successfully resolves a fundamental, well-known trade-off (e.g., accuracy vs. computational cost, or fairness vs. efficiency) without severe sacrifice on either axis; score 0 if it merely improves one metric while tanking another.
proposals.rationale: The dense model favors elegant resolutions to fundamental conflicts. R11 achieves massive acceleration without irregular sparsity or accuracy loss, and R45 resolves the fairness vs. efficiency trade-off in federated learning. The scorecard may overlook the difficulty of resolving such trade-offs non-trivially.

proposals.name: Emergence of Interpretable Latent Dynamics
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the abstract explicitly demonstrates or visualizes that the model learns meaningful, interpretable, or naturally structured latent representations without being explicitly forced to; score 0 if the latent space is treated purely as a black box.
proposals.rationale: The dense model values models where structure naturally emerges. R16 discovers latent hierarchical structure without explicit boundary information, and R52 recovers subtask hierarchies from unstructured demonstrations. The organic emergence of structure is a powerful indicator of conceptual depth.

proposals.name: Deterministic Algorithmic Substitution
proposals.instruction: Score 10 if the method replaces heuristic, slow, or approximate procedures with deterministic, provably optimal, or exact algorithmic steps (e.g., sampling-free inference); score 0 if it introduces more stochasticity or relies on unstable heuristics.
proposals.rationale: The dense model credits papers that provide exact, deterministic alternatives to historically messy probabilistic problems. R31 proposes sampling-free learning for Bayesian quantized networks to reduce variance, and R14 provides a deterministic algorithm for testing local optimality in ReLU networks.

proposals.name: Raw formatting and LaTeX residue
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (clean, rendered text) to 10 (pervasive unrendered LaTeX commands, stray hyphens, or copy-paste artifacts such as a placeholder). Measure only the extent of formatting artifacts; do not judge whether they harm readability.
proposals.rationale: Formatting residue is a production artifact unrelated to research quality but can affect a model's perception of polish. R23 contains raw LaTeX markup, R45 has a line-break artifact ('unstruc-tured'), and R52 is a placeholder ('International audience').

proposals.name: Abstract word count and verbosity
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (title-only or fewer than 30 words) to 10 (extremely long, e.g., >300 words). Measure only length; do not judge whether the abstract is well-written or poorly written.
proposals.rationale: Verbosity can inflate a scorecard by hitting more criteria, while brevity may be penalized despite equivalent insight. R19 is a very long low/high abstract, whereas R52 is a high/low item with almost no body text.

proposals.name: Density of exact quantitative claims
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (no specific numbers) to 10 (dense with exact percentages, benchmark scores, or multipliers like 14.4% or 5x). Count only explicit numerical figures; do not judge whether the results are impressive.
proposals.rationale: The number of exact performance figures can impress a criterion-based model independently of the work's significance. R13 and R30 report many exact gains, while R39 and R33 contain none.

proposals.name: Presence of external resource links
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (no URL or repository mentioned) to 10 (explicit URL plus statement of public code or data availability). Score only the presence and prominence of links; do not judge whether the resources are good.
proposals.rationale: Links to code or data can signal reproducibility but are not themselves research quality. R07 and R13 include GitHub links, while R39 and R52 mention none.

proposals.name: Coined method acronyms
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (no novel acronyms or coined method names) to 10 (multiple invented acronyms such as SSFG or Fixup). Count only new proper-noun method labels; do not judge whether the names are well-chosen.
proposals.rationale: Branding a method with an acronym can inflate perceived novelty without indicating underlying merit. R19 introduces SSFG, MSSFG and PSSFG; R20 introduces Fixup.

proposals.name: Conformity to mainstream benchmark vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (no reference to standard ML benchmarks) to 10 (the abstract is dominated by mentions of ImageNet, CIFAR, WMT, MNIST, etc.). Score only the prevalence of standard benchmark names; do not judge whether the evaluation is rigorous.
proposals.rationale: Using familiar benchmark names can satisfy a checklist criterion regardless of the contribution's depth. R12 and R53 lean heavily on standard benchmarks, while R39 and R47 use domain-specific or theoretical constructs.

proposals.name: Announcement of new dataset or benchmark
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (no new dataset introduced) to 10 (the abstract's primary contribution is a new dataset or benchmark). Score only the extent to which a new resource is announced; do not judge whether the dataset is valuable.
proposals.rationale: Introducing a new dataset can attract attention and satisfy a contribution criterion without implying methodological innovation. R16, R29 and R47 each introduce a new dataset.

proposals.name: Late-arriving synthesis positioning
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (self-contained problem with no reference to prior methods) to 10 (the abstract explicitly frames itself against many existing baselines or prior limitations). Score only the degree of crowded-conversation framing; do not judge whether the positioning is accurate.
proposals.rationale: An abstract that reads as a late entry into a crowded field may score differently from an early, self-contained one. R40 and R44 explicitly enumerate many prior approaches, whereas R39 presents a self-contained theoretical result.

proposals.name: Superlative or state-of-the-art language
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (neutral language) to 10 (pervasive use of phrases like state-of-the-art, unprecedented, or significantly outperforms). Count only superlative phrases; do not judge whether the claims are justified.
proposals.rationale: Strong promotional language can bias a reader or model toward higher scores independently of substance. R04 claims 'above human-level performance'; R53 uses 'unprecedented quality'.

proposals.name: Mathematical notation density
proposals.instruction: Score from 0 (no mathematical symbols or formalism) to 10 (dense with inline symbols, norms, sets, and equations). Score only the amount of mathematical notation visible in the text; do not judge whether the math is correct.
proposals.rationale: Heavy mathematical notation can either impress or alienate a model independently of the work's significance. R02 and R32 contain dense formalism, while R46 contains almost none.
